claims.text: The initial material is a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous microstructure.
At 700°C, simultaneous wear and corrosion accelerate coupled degradation relative to separate wear or corrosion exposures.
Thermally activated diffusion is a primary mediator of the accelerated degradation.
Mechanical stress induces microstructural evolution during simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Thermally activated diffusion and stress-induced microstructural evolution act synergistically.
The proposed synergy enhances the formation of corrosive, wear-induced defects.
The proposed microstructural changes facilitate ingress of corrosive species into the alloy.
Simultaneous exposure will increase total degradation by 30% relative to a matched separate-exposure baseline.
Simultaneous exposure will increase wear rate by 25% relative to the wear-only baseline.
Simultaneous exposure will increase corrosion rate by 40% relative to the corrosion-only baseline.
The simultaneous-exposure condition has a wear rate of 10^-4 mm/s.
The simultaneous-exposure condition has a corrosion rate of 10^-6 g/cm^2/s.
High-temperature scanning electron microscopy or in situ X-ray diffraction can monitor relevant microstructural and compositional evolution during degradation.
A total-degradation increase of no more than 20% under simultaneous exposure falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Wear rate is specified as a fixed exposure condition of 10^-4 mm/s but is also treated as a response predicted to increase by 25%; it cannot simultaneously be controlled at that value and serve as an unconstrained outcome.

Corrosion rate is specified as a fixed exposure condition of 10^-6 g/cm^2/s but is also treated as a response predicted to increase by 40%; it cannot simultaneously be fixed and measured as the predicted response.
